title: What does the insurer pay out?
hook: Each house pays $120 a year against a 1-in-100 risk. What does that risk cost?

doesNotKnow: how to find the average payout (chance × loss)
why paying more than the average loss can still be sensible

misconception: If insurance costs more than the average loss, it is a rip-off.
objective: The learner can compute an expected loss as chance times size, explain that a premium above it covers the insurer's costs, and explain that insurance swaps a small certain cost for protection from a rare large loss that a pool of many customers can absorb.

claims.text: A 1-in-100 chance a year of a $10,000 loss means an average payout of $100 per customer a year.
A $120 premium is $20 above the average loss; in this model that $20 covers the insurer's costs.
claims.source: 120 − 100 = 20. 'Covers the insurer's costs' is the model's assumption (brief), not a claim about real insurers' margins.

claims.text: With 100 independent houses, single years are lumpy: a year has no loss about 37% of the time and two or more about 26% of the time.

On the stage, one seeded run: the first year has exactly one loss, and over the first 101 years the average payout is $99 per customer a year; the stage's tally shows 36 years with no loss, 37 with one and 28 with two or more.
claims.source: Demo.tsx HISTORY with mulberry32(seed 1), one draw per house per year, loss if < 0.01. Seed 1 was CHOSEN because its first year has exactly one loss, as in the brief. Across 2,000 seeds the 101-year average is $100 on average, 95% between $80 and $120; for seed 1, every average from 50 to 1,001 years lies between $88 and $107. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node with the kit's mulberry32 (fc22-5/ins.mjs): seed 1 year 1 losses = [house 1]; first 101 years: 98 losses, average $99.01 (rounds to $99); tally 36 / 37 / 28 (sum 101). Source extras also reproduce: 2,000 seeds mean $100.02, 2.5-97.5% $80.2-$119.8; seed 1 averages from 50 to 1,001 years lie in $87.7-$107.1. The seed is disclosed as chosen.

claims.text: Insurance swaps a small certain cost (the premium every year) for cover against a rare large loss; no house knows in advance whether it will be hit, and the insurer can carry the losses because it pools many customers (here 100 houses).
claims.source: Risk pooling and risk aversion as the basis of insurance markets (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 27, 'The Market for Insurance'). Law of large numbers: the per-customer average over many independent risks approaches the expected loss. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Verified by derivation and the stage, not by the cited book: in the model a customer pays $120 every year and is paid $10,000 when hit (swap of a small sure cost for a rare large loss). Pooling: per-customer yearly payout SD is sqrt(0.01 x 0.99) x $10,000 = $995 for one house and $99.5 averaged over 100 independent houses; the stage's average settles near $100. Mankiw not opened; the cited title is inexact (web search: the section is 'The Markets for Insurance' inside ch. 27 'The Basic Tools of Finance', edition-dependent). Non-blocking citation fix for the builder. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal reworded: 'No house knows which it will be: each swaps a small sure cost for cover against a rare large loss, which the pool of 100 carries.'. Unverified.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: independent risks, no fraud, one premium; it gives no advice about buying cover.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own simulation, shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

claims.text: "Your house" (outlined, house 0) pays $120 every year; in the seeded run it is never hit in the first 101 years, so it pays $12,120 in premiums and cover pays it nothing. Seed 1 was kept; house 0 was chosen because never being hit is the commonest outcome in this run (40 of 100 houses).
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14, scratchpad b5x/ins.mjs, same mulberry32 and loop as Demo.tsx): seed 1, house index 0 has 0 losses in years 1-101. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v3 replaces the lucky house (index 1, hit in year 1 and twice in 101 years) with house 0. Unverified.

claims.text: In the seeded run, over the first 101 years, 40 of the 100 houses are never hit, 33 are hit once and 27 are hit twice or more.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14, scratchpad b5x/ins.mjs, same mulberry32 seed 1 and loop as Demo.tsx): per-house loss counts over years 1-101 give 0: 40, 1: 33, 2: 15, 3+: 12. Shown on stage as 'Houses hit 0 / 1 / 2+ times' and quoted in the reveal from the learner's longest run. Unverified.

recall.question: A phone has a 1-in-20 chance a year of a $400 repair. A plan costs $30 a year. What is the average repair cost per phone a year?
recall.why: Average loss = chance × size = 1/20 × $400 = $20. The $30 plan is $10 above it: you pay that for not facing the $400 surprise.
